questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=3t,\,y=4t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)=3 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3t\sqrt{{(3)}^{2}+{(4)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3t\sqrt{25}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}3t\cdot 5\,\text{d}t \\  & =30\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y={2}^{t},\,t\in [0,3].
$$

What integral gives the surface area generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({2}^{t})={2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{{(2t)}^{2}+{({2}^{t}\operatorname{ln}⁡2)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{2}^{2t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+{4}^{t}{ln}^{2}⁡2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\frac{1}{2}t,\,y=\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2},\,t\in [0,\sqrt{3}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt{3}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}t)=\frac{1}{2}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2}t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}(1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\frac{1}{2}t\cdot \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+{t}^{2}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $4$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}\cdot 2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}[(4)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(8-1) \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 7π6

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x={t}^{2},\,y=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4},\,t\in [0,\sqrt[4]{6}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi x\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}x\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=0$ to ${t}_{2}=\sqrt[4]{6}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{4})=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}{t}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+\frac{16}{3}{t}^{6}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\sqrt{4{t}^{2}(1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4})}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}{t}^{2}\cdot 2|t|\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{16}{3}{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t⟹{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{16}\text{d}u.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $0$ | $\sqrt[4]{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =4\pi {\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[4]{6}}\sqrt{1+\frac{4}{3}{t}^{4}}\cdot {t}^{3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{3}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}{u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}\cdot {[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}[(9)^{3/2}-(1)^{3/2}] \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}(27-1) \\  & =13\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: 13π

questions.problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as 

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2})),\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{\pi }{2}].
$$

Determine the surface area $S$ generated when this curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis. Do not round the answer.

$S=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since our curve is given in parametric form, we have

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${t}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{3}$ to ${t}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

Computing the derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡(t/2)}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{t}{2})\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{csc}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{(\operatorname{csc}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}+{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-2+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{csc}^{2}⁡t-1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{{cot}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate the last integral using the substitution $u=\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.$ We also update the limits of integration for $u:$

| **$t$** | $\frac{\pi }{3}$ | $\frac{\pi }{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ | $1$ |

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1}2\pi \,\text{d}u \\  & =2\pi {[u]}_{\sqrt{3}/2}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =\pi (2-\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

fields.input_html: π(2−3)
